# Simulated example {#sec-quickstart}

```{r}
#| label: sim-setup
library(sconjoint)
house <- "#004a8c"
truth <- simconjoint_truth$population
tv <- function(name) truth$value[truth$name == name]
t_start <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
```

The package's `simconjoint` data contain 800 simulated respondents who each choose between two
candidates ten times. Their underlying tastes are known. In this simulated population, for
example, `r round(100 * tv("share: prefer Republican"), 1)`% prefers a Republican candidate to an
otherwise identical Democrat, and long experience raises a candidate's chance of being chosen by
`r round(100 * tv("AME: long vs no experience"), 1)` percentage points on average. This chapter runs
the whole workflow on these data and compares the resulting estimates with the truth.

All results below come from one illustrative run that executes live in about five minutes on a
recent laptop. It uses a small network and fewer integration nodes than the paper; while the
paper's larger settings reduce integration and fitting error, they do not guarantee narrower
intervals.

## Experiment

Each candidate is described by four attributes drawn at random and independently---party,
experience, policy position, and gender---and the data store one row per candidate, or two rows per
task.

```{r}
#| label: sim-data
head(simconjoint, 4)
```

Alongside the candidate profiles, each respondent has three characteristics: age, ideology on a
seven-point scale from $-3$ (very liberal) to 3 (very conservative), and gender.

Preparing the profiles takes two steps. First, `sc_design()` describes how the candidates were
drawn and codes each attribute as one 0/1 indicator per level other than the first, yielding six
coded features in all. Next, `sc_code()` turns the two candidates of each task into their
difference, first minus second.

```{r}
#| label: sim-design
des <- sc_design(list(party = c("Democrat", "Republican"),
                      experience = c("none", "some", "long"),
                      position = c("liberal", "moderate", "conservative"),
                      gender = c("male", "female")), tasks = 10)
des
A <- simconjoint[simconjoint$profile == 1, ]          # first (left) candidate of each task
B <- simconjoint[simconjoint$profile == 2, ]
X <- sc_code(des, A, B)
head(X, 3)
```

To assemble the inputs for estimation, `sc_data()` collects the choices (coded 1 when the first
candidate was chosen), the coded feature differences, the respondent ids, and the characteristics
that predict mean tastes. Attaching the design here allows `sc_states()` to average later over the
comparisons each respondent could have seen.

```{r}
#| label: sim-scdata
Z <- as.matrix(A[!duplicated(A$id), c("age", "ideology", "female")])
rownames(Z) <- unique(A$id)
x <- sc_data(A$chosen, X, A$id, Z = Z, groups = data.frame(female = Z[, "female"]), design = des,
             orientation = "y = 1 selects the first (left) candidate; X = first minus second")
x
```

## Truth

The simulated choices follow the package's model (@sec-intro): each respondent has tastes
$\beta_i = \mu(Z_i) + \Lambda u_i$ with two taste factors, along with an individual pull
$a_i = \sqrt{\omega}\, v_i$ toward the left candidate on top of the average pull $\kappa$, where
$\kappa = 0.2$ and $\omega = 0.3$.

Across respondent characteristics, the taste for a Republican rises with ideology and flattens out
for strong partisans, while older respondents value experience more. Policy tastes follow a
quadratic loss around the respondent's own position, meaning a candidate loses utility the farther
its position is from the respondent's. As for the two taste factors, the first moves party and
policy, whereas the second moves experience and gender. Every formula is given in `?simconjoint`.

```{r}
#| label: sim-truth
simconjoint_truth$parameters[c("kappa", "omega")]
simconjoint_truth$parameters$loading
```

True population values are stored in `simconjoint_truth$population`. Each entry is an exact sum
over the finite set of characteristic values, with the integrals inside the sum computed by
quadrature to an accuracy of about $10^{-6}$ or better.

## Fits

Using five-fold splitting, `sc_fit()` estimates the model once per fold, each time training on the
other four folds. The code below fits specifications with one, two, and three taste factors, each
with one hidden layer of 8 units, one start, at most 100 epochs, and Sobol rules of 128 to 256
nodes.

```{r}
#| label: sim-fit
small <- list(hidden = 8L, seeds = 1L, control = list(max_epochs = 100L, patience = 5L),
              nodes = 128L, check_nodes = 256L, heldout_nodes = 256L, verbose = FALSE)
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fits <- lapply(1:3, function(q) do.call(sc_fit, c(list(x, q = q), small)))
t_fit <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

## Number of factors

To choose the number of taste factors, `sc_select_rank()` scores each fit on the respondents it did
not train on, moving from $q - 1$ to $q$ factors only when the held-out log score gains more than
two standard errors.

```{r}
#| label: sim-rank
rank <- sc_select_rank(fits)
rank
fit <- fits[[which(rank$selected)]]
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-rank-text
#| echo: false
q_sel <- rank$q[rank$selected]
```

Here the rule picks $q = `r q_sel`$`r if (q_sel == 2) ", the true number" else ", not the true number, 2"`.
Adding a second factor improves the held-out score by `r round(rank$z[2], 1)` standard errors,
whereas a third changes it by `r round(rank$z[3], 1)`, which is noise. Two factors are needed
because respondents with the same characteristics still differ in two ways: how strongly partisan
they are, and how much they care about experience and gender.

## Fold states

Next, `sc_states()` computes what the estimator needs from each fold's fit. The slow part is each
held-out respondent's information, which is evaluated as an average over task sets drawn from
`des`, the design carried by `x`. Here the code uses 40 draws per respondent, compared with 250 to
300 in the paper.

```{r}
#| label: sim-states
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
st <- sc_states(fit, M = 40L, ny = 4L, info_nodes = 256L, score_nodes = 512L)
t_states <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
st
```

## Estimates

Each target in the list below names one population quantity (@sec-quantities). Beyond simple means
and preference shares, the list includes a compensating share---the share of respondents for whom
party outweighs experience, taking a Republican with no experience over a Democrat with long
experience---and a contest comparing a moderate Republican woman with long experience to a liberal
Democrat man with some experience, with position effects set to zero. For the remaining summaries,
`sc_ame_switch()` and `sc_importance(des)` draw their contexts and attributes directly from the
design.

```{r}
#| label: sim-estimate
contest <- sc_code(des, data.frame(party = "Republican", experience = "long", position = "moderate", gender = "female"),
                   data.frame(party = "Democrat", experience = "some", position = "liberal", gender = "male"))
targets <- list(
  sc_mean("mean: Republican", "party_Republican"),
  sc_mean("mean: long experience", "experience_long"),
  sc_mean("mean: conservative position", "position_conservative"),
  sc_mean("mean: female candidate", "gender_female"),
  sc_share("share: prefer Republican", "party_Republican"),
  sc_share("share: prefer long experience", "experience_long"),
  sc_share("share: prefer female candidate", "gender_female"),
  sc_share("share: Republican without experience over Democrat with long",
           c(party_Republican = 1, experience_long = -1)),
  sc_contest("contest: A beats B", drop(contest)),
  sc_ame_switch("AME: long vs no experience", "experience", level = "long", ref = "none"),
  sc_importance(des, names = paste("importance:", names(des$attributes))))
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
est <- sc_estimate(st, targets)
t_est <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
est$truth <- truth$value[match(est$name, truth$name)]
est$covered <- est$truth >= est$lower & est$truth <= est$upper
knitr::kable(est[, c("name", "truth", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "covered")], digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Quantity", "Truth", "Estimate", "95% lower", "95% upper", "Covered"))
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-cover
#| echo: false
n_int <- sum(!is.na(est$covered)); n_cov <- sum(est$covered, na.rm = TRUE)
miss <- est$name[which(!est$covered)]
imp <- which(est$kind == "importance"); imp_worst <- imp[which.max(abs(est$estimate[imp] - est$truth[imp]))]
imp_err <- abs(est$estimate[imp_worst] - est$truth[imp_worst])
resp <- simconjoint_truth$respondents; law <- simconjoint_truth$covariate_law
cons_sample <- mean(resp$ideology > 0); cons_pop <- sum(law$ideology_probs[law$ideology > 0])
party_sample <- mean(simconjoint_truth$beta[, "party_Republican"])
r_party <- est[est$name == "mean: Republican", ]
```

Across these targets, `r n_cov` of the `r n_int` intervals cover the truth`r if (length(miss)) paste0("; the miss", if (length(miss) > 1) "es are " else " is ", paste0("\"", miss, "\"", collapse = ", ")) else ""`.
Because 95% intervals are expected to miss about once in twenty times, a single run cannot show
that coverage is exact.

Furthermore, the intervals target the population rather than the sample, and this sample of 800
leans right: it holds more conservatives than the population (`r round(100 * cons_sample)`% against
`r round(100 * cons_pop)`%), and its true average taste for a Republican is
`r round(party_sample, 2)` compared with `r round(r_party$truth, 2)` in the population. The
interval for that mean, from `r round(r_party$lower, 2)` to `r round(r_party$upper, 2)`,
`r if (isTRUE(r_party$covered)) "covers the population value" else "covers the sample's value but not the population's"`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-estimates
#| fig-cap: "Estimates and 95% intervals (blue) against the truth (open circles)"
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 5
short <- c("Republican", "Long experience", "Conservative position", "Female candidate",
           "Prefer Republican", "Prefer long experience", "Prefer female candidate",
           "Rep., no exp., over Dem., long exp.", "Contest: A beats B", "AME: long experience",
           paste("Importance:", names(des$attributes)))
lab <- setNames(short, est$name)
truth_of <- setNames(est$truth, est$name)
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), 2, byrow = TRUE), widths = c(1, 1.6), heights = c(4, .45))
sc_plot_estimates(est[1:4, ], labels = lab, reference = truth_of, reference_style = "circle",
                  xlim = c(-.3, .9), xlab = "Mean taste (logit scale)", legend = FALSE)
sc_plot_estimates(est[5:14, ], labels = lab, reference = truth_of, reference_style = "circle",
                  xlim = c(0, .85), xlab = "Share or probability", legend = FALSE,
                  groups = rep(c("Shares", "Contest", "AME", "Importance"), c(4, 1, 1, 4)))
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
keys <- c("Estimate and 95% interval", "Truth", "No interval")
legend("center", keys, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", pch = c(16, 1, 1), lty = c(1, NA, NA),
       col = c(house, "black", house), pt.cex = c(.8, 1.2, .8), cex = .85,
       text.width = strwidth(paste0(keys, "mm"), cex = .85))
```

In the figure, the left panel plots mean tastes while the right panel displays shares,
probabilities, the AME, and importance shares, grouped by kind. Importance shares carry no intervals, and in this
run their largest miss is `r round(100 * imp_err, 1)` points, for
`r sub("importance: ", "", est$name[imp_worst])`, so they should be read as rough.

@fig-sim-shares shows the four preference shares another way: for each, the percent of respondents
who favor the contrast (blue, right) and the percent who oppose it (red, left), with the share's 95%
interval and the true share as an open circle. In this run,
`r k <- sum(est$covered[est$kind == "share"]); if (k == 4) "all four intervals cover" else paste(k, "of the four intervals cover")`
the truth.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-shares
#| fig-cap: "Shares favoring and opposing, with the truth"
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 3.4
sh <- est[est$kind == "share", ]
sc_plot_shares(sh, labels = lab, reference = truth_of[sh$name], reference_label = "Truth",
               groups = c("One attribute", "One attribute", "One attribute", "Trade-off"))
```

Although two population mean tastes---for party and policy---sit close to zero, that does not mean
respondents do not care (@fig-sim-laws).

## Taste distributions

For any taste, `sc_fitted_law()` returns each held-out respondent's fitted normal distribution---its
fitted law---with mean $c^\top\mu(Z_i)$ and standard deviation $\lVert\Lambda^\top c\rVert$. Mixing
these respondent-level distributions gives the fitted population distribution, whereas the true
distribution uses the true $\mu$ and $\Lambda$. The figure draws all six tastes on one axis,
grouped by attribute, with the true distribution in black and a vertical line at each corrected
mean.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-laws
#| fig-cap: "Fitted (blue) and true (black) distributions of the six tastes"
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 7
L0 <- simconjoint_truth$parameters$loading; mu0 <- simconjoint_truth$mu
sf <- des$features
true_law <- function(f) function(v)          # the true density: a mixture over respondents
  rowMeans(outer(v, mu0[, f], function(g, m) dnorm(g, m, sqrt(sum(L0[f, ]^2)))))
means6 <- sc_estimate(st, lapply(sf, function(f) sc_mean(f, f)))
sc_plot_laws(lapply(sf, function(f) sc_fitted_law(st, f)),
             labels = c("Republican", "Some experience", "Long experience", "Moderate position",
                        "Conservative position", "Female candidate"),
             truth = lapply(sf, true_law), means = means6,
             groups = c("Party", "Experience", "Experience", "Position", "Position", "Gender"),
             height = 1.3, bins = 300, outline = "line", xlim = c(-5, 5), xlab = "Taste (logit scale)")
```

For a Republican candidate, the true taste distribution has two humps, with liberals below zero and
conservatives above. The fitted distribution captures the right width, from about $-3$ to $3$, but
blurs those humps into a plateau. Because the 8-unit network learns a mean taste that is almost
linear in ideology while the truth---$2 \tanh(3s)$, with $s$ equal to ideology divided by
3---levels off away from the center, the fit compensates with a larger spread (shown in the table
below).

A network with two hidden layers (16 and 8 units) found the humps in our trials, yet it predicted
held-out choices worse, so the held-out score prefers the smoother fit; a better held-out score
therefore does not validate the fitted distribution. Even so, the shares stay close to the truth
because they depend mostly on the mass above zero, and the means remain close too, though the
larger spread absorbs part of the error in the mean`r if (!isTRUE(r_party$covered)) ", and in this run the interval for the Republican mean misses the population value" else ""`.

By contrast, the taste for long experience has a single hump, with about three quarters of it above
zero, and the fit recovers it almost exactly.

Turning to that spread, the loading $\Lambda$ itself is not identified, because any rotation of its
columns gives the same model. What is identified is the spread of tastes among respondents with the
same characteristics, $\Lambda\Lambda^\top$, and the square roots of its diagonal entries give the
conditional standard deviations. Averaged over the five folds, the fitted values compare with the
truth as follows:

```{r}
#| label: sim-spread
sd_fit <- rowMeans(sapply(st$folds, function(f) sqrt(rowSums(as.matrix(f$th$loading)^2))))
spread <- data.frame(feature = des$features, true_sd = round(sqrt(rowSums(L0^2)), 2),
                     fitted_sd = round(sd_fit, 2), row.names = NULL)
spread
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-spread-text
#| echo: false
gap <- abs(spread$fitted_sd - spread$true_sd); j <- which.max(gap)
```

For five of the six features, the fitted spread lies within `r round(max(gap[-j]), 2)` of the
truth. The exception is `r spread$feature[j]` (`r spread$fitted_sd[j]` against
`r spread$true_sd[j]`), where the spread absorbs the part of the mean taste the network did not
learn.

## Individual respondents

`sc_posterior()` combines the fitted law with a respondent's own choices, using the fold that did not train on the respondent (@sec-respondents).
The `history` argument sets how many of the first tasks to use.

```{r}
#| label: sim-posterior
b_true <- simconjoint_truth$beta[, "party_Republican"]
post <- lapply(c(0, 2, 5, 10), function(h)
  sc_posterior(st, contrasts = c(party_Republican = 1), history = h, nodes = 1024)$contrasts)
data.frame(tasks_used = c(0, 2, 5, 10),
           correlation = round(sapply(post, function(p) cor(p$mean, b_true)), 3),
           rmse = round(sapply(post, function(p) sqrt(mean((p$mean - b_true)^2))), 3))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mean against true taste for a Republican"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (j in c(1, 4))
  sc_plot_posterior(post[[j]], truth = b_true, xlab = "True taste for a Republican",
                    main = c("No tasks used", "", "", "All 10 tasks")[j])
par(op)
```

When no tasks are used, the posterior mean reduces to the fitted $\mu(Z_i)$, which already tracks
the true taste because ideology explains much of party taste. Adding all ten tasks raises the
correlation from `r round(cor(post[[1]]$mean, b_true), 2)` to
`r round(cor(post[[4]]$mean, b_true), 2)`, yet the points still scatter widely because ten choices
carry limited information and the posterior pulls each respondent toward $\mu(Z_i)$.

For that reason, the posterior is a prediction of a respondent's taste rather than a measurement of
it. Population questions, such as how many prefer a Republican, should therefore be answered with
the population targets above rather than counts of posterior means.

## What is recovered

```{r}
#| label: sim-recovered
#| echo: false
mean_miss <- miss[grepl("^mean: ", miss)]
n_mean <- sum(grepl("^mean: ", est$name))
```

Summarizing across the chapter, the list below describes this one run on one simulated sample; it
illustrates the workflow rather than validating the method.

- **Recovered:** the number of taste factors; the shares, compensating share, contest probability,
  AME, and `r if (length(mean_miss)) paste(n_mean - length(mean_miss), "of the", n_mean) else "all"`
  mean tastes, with `r n_cov` of `r n_int` intervals covering the population value; the
  distribution of the taste for experience; the spread of most tastes; and the position effects
  $\kappa$ and $\omega$ (whose per-fold values appear in `summary(fit)`).
- **Recovered roughly:** `r if (length(mean_miss)) paste0(paste0("the mean taste for a ", sub("mean: ", "", mean_miss), collapse = " and "), ", whose interval misses the population value: the sample leans right, and the larger spread absorbs part of the error in the mean; ") else ""`importance
  shares, which carry no intervals and miss here by up to `r round(100 * imp_err, 1)` points; and
  the distribution of the taste for a Republican, which has the right width but blurs its two humps
  into a plateau.
- **Not recovered:** the loading $\Lambda$ itself, which is identified only up to rotation; and
  individual tastes, which ten tasks pin down only partly.

```{r}
#| label: sim-time
#| echo: false
t_total <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t_start
```

In total, this chapter took `r round(t_total / 60, 1)` minutes to run: `r round(t_fit / 60, 1)`
minutes for the three fits, `r round(t_states / 60, 1)` for the fold states, and
`r round(t_est / 60, 1)` for the estimates.

## Next steps

Starting from saved fits, @sec-gs and @sec-br apply this same workflow to the paper's data, while
@sec-quantities lists every target. For another experiment with independently drawn attributes,
describe it with `sc_design()` and code its profiles with `sc_code()`; every step above then works
unchanged.
